options.text: Azure Event Hubs publishes NO consumer-lag metric. When the Abstract consumer stalls, incoming messages keep flowing, no error is raised, every health dashboard stays green, and message retention quietly expires the backlog — after which the data is gone permanently. These alerts infer the stall from outgoing traffic collapsing while incoming traffic continues. Without them, that failure is effectively undetectable.

basics.name: namespaceName
basics.label: Event Hubs namespace to monitor
basics.toolTip: Name of the EXISTING namespace. Deploy the Event Hub source template first — this one only adds alerts.

validations.message: 6-50 characters, must start with a letter and end with a letter or number.

basics.name: alertPrefix
basics.label: Alert rule name prefix
basics.toolTip: Prefix for every alert rule created here. Pick something recognisable so operators know not to delete them by hand.

basics.name: actionGroupId
basics.label: Action Group resource ID (who gets notified)
basics.toolTip: Full resource ID of an existing Action Group. Leave empty to create the rules without notifications — they will appear in Azure Monitor but nobody will be told when they fire.

validations.message: Leave empty, or supply a full Action Group resource ID.

options.text: No Action Group supplied. The alert rules will be created and will evaluate, but NOBODY WILL BE NOTIFIED when they fire. That is rarely what you want for a data-loss alert — supply an Action Group, or plan to attach one afterwards.

basics.name: createDisabled
basics.label: Create the rules disabled, for review first
basics.toolTip: Useful on a noisy estate: deploy, read the thresholds, then enable.

options.text: Defaults are deliberately conservative — they are meant to catch a real outage without paging anyone over a quiet afternoon. Tune the stall window to comfortably exceed the Abstract consumer's poll interval.

elements.name: consumerStallWindowMinutes
elements.label: Consumer stall window (minutes)
elements.toolTip: How long outgoing traffic must stay collapsed before the consumer is considered stalled. Too short and a normal quiet period pages someone; too long and you burn retention before anyone knows.

elements.name: minIncomingToAlert
elements.label: Minimum incoming messages before a flat consumer counts as stalled
elements.toolTip: Guards against alerting on a genuinely idle hub, where zero-in and zero-out is correct and healthy.

elements.name: ingestionStoppedWindowMinutes
elements.label: Ingestion stopped window (minutes)
elements.toolTip: Zero incoming messages for this long means the PRODUCER side broke — a deleted diagnostic setting, a revoked Send key, or a firewall change that blocked Azure Monitor's own delivery.

elements.name: throttleThreshold
elements.label: Throttled requests per 5 minutes before alerting
elements.toolTip: Any sustained throttling means throughput units are saturated. Note partitions cap parallelism independently and cannot be increased on Standard.

elements.name: dataLossSeverity
elements.label: Severity for data-loss alerts
elements.toolTip: Applies to the consumer-stalled and ingestion-stopped rules. These are the two that lose data permanently, so they warrant a higher severity than the capacity alerts.

elements.name: capacitySeverity
elements.label: Severity for capacity alerts
elements.toolTip: Applies to throttling, user errors and quota-exceeded. These degrade the pipeline but do not silently destroy data.

options.text: The Auto-Inflate COST ratchet is deliberately not alerted on here. Auto-Inflate scales throughput units up and never scales them back down, so one traffic spike sets a permanent new floor on the bill — and because Capture is metered per throughput unit, it inflates that line too. There is no platform metric for the provisioned throughput-unit count; the scale events land in the AutoScaleLogs diagnostic category, which needs a diagnostic setting on the namespace itself sending to a Log Analytics workspace. This template cannot assume that exists. Until it is wired up, review provisioned throughput units by hand each month.

Why the consumer-stall rule is a log search and not a metric alert: Event Hubs metrics are sparse. When nothing is consuming, the platform may emit no outgoing datapoints at all rather than emitting zeros — so a metric alert of the form 'outgoing < threshold' has nothing to evaluate and sits in Insufficient Data forever. The KQL used here synthesises a zero row when the metric is silent, which makes 'no data' and 'zero throughput' the same alertable condition.
